title: Reverse Digits
statement:
Reverse the decimal digits of a 32-bit signed integer, returning 0 if the result does not fit in 32 bits.

Contract
- Reverse the digits of the absolute value and keep the original sign. Trailing zeros of the input become leading zeros and vanish, so `120` becomes `21`.
- If the reversed value is outside the range of `int` (below `-2147483648` or above `2147483647`), return `0`.
- `0` returns `0`. `Integer.MIN_VALUE` reverses to something too large, so it returns `0`.
- Do not use `long`, `double`, `BigInteger`, or strings to hold the reversed number; detect the overflow before it happens using `int` arithmetic only.

Examples
- `reverseDigits(1203)` returns `3021`.
- `reverseDigits(-450)` returns `-54`.
- `reverseDigits(1563847412)` returns `0`, because the reversal `2147483651` exceeds `2147483647`.
hints: Peel the last digit with `x % 10`, drop it with `x / 10`, and push it onto the result with `result * 10 + digit`. In Java the remainder of a negative number is negative, so the sign takes care of itself.

The danger is the multiply-and-add overflowing silently. Instead of checking afterwards (too late with plain `int`), check before pushing the digit whether `result` is already past `limit / 10`, or exactly at it with a digit beyond the limit's last digit.

Test both ends: `result > MAX / 10`, or `result == MAX / 10` with `digit > 7`; and `result < MIN / 10`, or `result == MIN / 10` with `digit < -8`. Intended complexity: O(1) time (at most 10 loop iterations per call, so the probe measures a batch of calls) and O(1) space.
